title: COS_102 — End of Semester Objective Exam

questions.q: Which sequence gives the four steps to problem-solving in the correct order?
options: Understand the problem; carry out the solution plan; create a solution step-by-step plan; evaluate and refactor the solution
Create a solution step-by-step plan; understand the problem; carry out the solution plan; evaluate and refactor the solution
Understand the problem; create a solution step-by-step plan; carry out the solution plan; evaluate and refactor the solution
Understand the problem; create a solution step-by-step plan; evaluate and refactor the solution; carry out the solution plan
questions.why: Why C is right: the four steps are, in order, understand the problem; create a solution step-by-step plan; carry out the solution plan; evaluate and refactor the solution. Why the others are wrong: A swaps steps 2 and 3, so the plan is carried out before it exists · B puts planning before understanding, the single commonest reversal · D moves evaluation before execution, although there is nothing to evaluate until the plan has been carried out.

questions.q: Which three questions must be answered while understanding a problem?
options: What are the inputs? What are the processes involved? What is the output?
What data do we have? Where is the data? What formulas are related to the problem?
Can we derive the result differently? Can we improve the performance? How have other people solved it?
Who will implement the algorithm? How much knowledge does that person have? What are the computer specifications?
questions.why: Why A is right: understanding the problem means answering what the inputs are, what processes are involved, and what the output is — the input–process–output triple. Why the others are wrong: B is the *starting point* list from step 2 of the week 4 algorithm development process · C is the list of refactoring questions from step 4 · D is the stepwise-refinement list from step 4 of algorithm development.

questions.q: Which statement about translators is correct?
options: An interpreter converts assembly language into machine code
A compiler converts assembly language into machine code
An assembler converts a high-level language into machine code directly
A compiler converts a high-level language into assembly language
questions.why: Why D is right: in this course a compiler converts a high-level language into assembly language. Why the others are wrong: A gives the interpreter the assembler's job — the interpreter converts high-level language into machine code directly · B gives the compiler the assembler's job · C gives the assembler the interpreter's job; the assembler works only from assembly language.

questions.q: Carrying out the solution plan entails four activities. Which list is correct?
options: Coding; problem analysis; debugging and testing; program documentation
Coding; compilation and execution; debugging and testing; program documentation
Coding; compilation and execution; debugging and testing; refactoring
Problem description; coding; algorithm review; program documentation
questions.why: Why B is right: carrying out the solution plan entails coding, compilation and execution, debugging and testing, and program documentation. Why the others are wrong: A imports problem analysis, which belongs to algorithm development, not to step 3 · C replaces documentation with refactoring, which is step 4, not step 3 · D mixes in problem description and algorithm review, both from the week 4 development process.

questions.q: How does debugging differ from testing?
options: Debugging verifies that the program works as expected, while testing finds errors so that they can be removed
Debugging finds errors so that they can be removed to avoid program failure, while testing verifies that the program works as expected
Debugging and testing are two names for the same activity, carried out after documentation
Debugging removes syntax errors only, while testing removes logical and run-time errors
questions.why: Why B is right: debugging finds errors so they can be removed to avoid program failure; testing verifies that the program works as expected. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two definitions, the standard swap · C denies the distinction the course draws and misplaces both after documentation · D invents a split by error type; neither activity is restricted to one of the three error types.

questions.q: Which statement about refactoring a solution is correct?
options: It changes the function of the solution so that the program produces better results
It adds new features to the solution while keeping the original structure
It is carried out before the solution works, to prevent errors from appearing
It leaves the function of the solution unchanged while improving its structure, design and efficiency
questions.why: Why D is right: refactoring does not change the function of the solution; it makes it more efficient while improving structure and design. Why the others are wrong: A says the function changes, which is exactly what refactoring never does · B confuses refactoring with adding features · C confuses refactoring with debugging; refactoring happens once a solution is already working.

questions.q: When does program documentation begin and end?
options: It starts at the problem analysis stage and continues to the testing stage
It starts at the coding stage and continues to the testing stage
It starts after testing is complete, so that the finished program is described
It starts at the problem analysis stage and ends when coding begins
questions.why: Why A is right: program documentation starts at the problem analysis stage and continues to the testing stage. Why the others are wrong: B starts it too late, at coding · C treats documentation as something written afterwards rather than a process running alongside development · D ends it too early, at coding, ignoring that it runs through testing.

questions.q: A lecturer asks a computer how many of 200 students scored above 70. This is an example of which type of computational problem?
options: A decision problem
A search problem
A counting problem
An optimization problem
questions.why: Why C is right: determining the number of values with a particular property is a counting problem. Why the others are wrong: A would fit "is there any student above 70?", whose answer is yes or no · B would fit "find a student who scored above 70", whose answer is a value with the property · D would fit "who scored highest?", where the best possible solution is wanted.

questions.q: The final-grade algorithm takes five grades, computes their average as the final grade, and prints "PASS" if the final grade reaches the pass mark of 45, otherwise "FAIL". The grades 40, 45, 50, 38 and 49 are entered. What is the final grade, and what is printed?
options: 44.4, and "PASS" is printed
55.5, and "PASS" is printed
222, and "PASS" is printed
44.4, and "FAIL" is printed
questions.why: Why D is right: 40 + 45 + 50 + 38 + 49 = 222, and 222 ÷ 5 = 44.4. The pass mark is 45, and 44.4 is below it, so "FAIL" is printed. *(The week 1 slide's flowchart tests `Is Grade > 44`, under which 44.4 would wrongly print "PASS". Write `Is Grade >= 45`.)* Why the others are wrong: A is what you get from the slide's faulty `Grade > 44` test · B divides the total by four instead of five · C compares the total 222 with the pass mark instead of the average.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT an attribute of routine problems?
options: It provides a question that needs an answer, in addition to some required facts or numbers
It can be solved with algorithms
It can usually be solved using various unconventional approaches
It is solely about identifying the most appropriate algorithm to apply
questions.why: Why C is right: unconventional approaches based on originality and creativity are an attribute of **non-routine** problems, so it is the odd one out here. Why the others are wrong: A, B and D are all listed attributes of routine problems — a question plus the required facts, solvability with algorithms, and the task being solely to pick the right algorithm.

questions.q: To solve a non-routine problem a novel method must be developed. What does that method involve?
options: Defining the problem and generating analogies; finding similarities and selecting one; using the description and similarities to generate ideas
Studying the problem critically; gathering relevant information; identifying and implementing an effective strategy
Identifying the nature and parameters of the problem; specifying the criteria for success; determining whether it can be grouped as a specific type
Checking the description for unstated assumptions; checking it for ambiguity; checking it for incompleteness
questions.why: Why B is right: the novel method is study the problem critically; gather relevant information; identify and implement an effective strategy. Why the others are wrong: A is the three steps of the **analogy** strategy · C is the three considerations of **problem recognition** from week 3 · D is the three issues that arise in **problem description** from week 4.

questions.q: Which of the following is a non-routine problem?
options: Give an approximate number of hairs on your head
Calculate the area of a 150 m by 2000 m parking space
Dan had $500 and now has $287; how much did he give his friend?
Find the average of five grades and decide whether the student passed
questions.why: Why A is right: there is no standard method for counting the hairs on a head, so it is non-routine — the lecture's own example. Why the others are wrong: B is an area calculation, solvable with one arithmetic operation, so routine · C is a subtraction, routine · D is an average and a comparison, routine. Difficulty is not the test; the existence of a standard method is.

questions.q: What does it mean to call a problem unsolvable?
options: No systematic method exists for deciding the general case, even though particular instances may still be worked out
No solution can possibly be found for any instance of the problem
A solution exists, but present-day computers are not fast enough to find it
The answer to the problem is always false, whatever the input
questions.why: Why A is right: "unsolvable" means no systematic method exists for the general case, not that solutions can never be found. Why the others are wrong: B is the everyday reading the lecture explicitly rejects — the substitution puzzle does come out, in three moves · C confuses unsolvability with slowness, which is a complexity issue, not a computability one · D confuses an unsolvable problem with a decision problem whose answer happens to be no.

questions.q: How are undecidable and unsolvable problems related?
options: Unsolvable problems are a subset of undecidable problems
Undecidable problems are a subset of unsolvable problems, restricted to those needing an accurate true or false answer for every input
The two terms mean exactly the same thing
Undecidable problems can be solved by the universal Turing machine, but only very slowly
questions.why: Why B is right: undecidable problems are a subset of unsolvable problems, restricted to those requiring an accurate true/false answer for every input. Why the others are wrong: A inverts the containment · C treats the two as synonyms, the most frequent error · D contradicts the definition; if the UTM could solve them, they would not be unsolvable.

questions.q: What were Turing's two most significant contributions to the advent of the modern computer?
options: Inventing the compiler, and showing that machine code can be generated from assembly language
Storing encoded instructions on punched tape, and proving that every mathematical problem is decidable
Storing encoded instructions in the computer's memory, and showing that a single machine of fixed structure can carry out every computation the UTM can carry out
Designing the central processing unit, and proving that the halting problem can be solved for finite programs
questions.why: Why C is right: the two contributions are storing encoded instructions in the computer's memory, and showing that a single machine of fixed structure can carry out every computation the UTM can. Why the others are wrong: A credits Turing with the compiler, which belongs to the week 1 translator material · B keeps instructions on tape rather than in memory — the tape is how the UTM reads a program, not the contribution — and claims universal decidability, which Turing disproved · D attributes hardware design to him and reverses the halting-problem result.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the problem-solving strategies taught in this course?
options: Means–ends analysis
Analogy
Heuristics
Brute force
questions.why: Why D is right: brute force is one of the five **sophisticated computational approaches** of week 3, not one of the problem-solving strategies of week 2. Why the others are wrong: A, B and C are all among the six strategies (brainstorming, heuristics, trial and error, means–ends analysis, abstraction, analogy). *(The week 2 summary names only the first four; if an item asks how many strategies there are, the examiner may key four.)*

questions.q: A restaurant owner has three possible suppliers and can afford to trial each one for a month before deciding. Which strategy does the course describe as suitable here, and why?
options: Heuristics, because a sub-optimal solution is acceptable
Brainstorming, because the ideas of other people can be fine-tuned
Trial and error, because the number of possible solutions is few
Means–ends analysis, because the problem is broken into smaller problems
questions.why: Why C is right: trial and error is recommended where the number of possible solutions is few, and three suppliers each trialled in turn is exactly that. Why the others are wrong: A describes heuristics, where a decision is made without stopping to evaluate; here each supplier *is* evaluated · B describes brainstorming, which generates ideas rather than testing candidates that already exist · D describes means–ends analysis, which breaks a problem into sub-problems; nothing is being decomposed here.

questions.q: The London Underground map illustrates one strategy. Which one, and what is the product of applying it called?
options: Analogy, and the product is called an analogue
Heuristics, and the product is called a rule of thumb
Means–ends analysis, and the product is called a sub-problem
Abstraction, and the product is called a model
questions.why: Why D is right: the map filters out the unneeded attribute — geographic accuracy — so abstraction is the strategy, and the essential idea it forms is called a model. Why the others are wrong: A confuses abstraction with analogy, which reuses understanding of a *different* system · B confuses it with heuristics; a map is not a rule of thumb · C confuses it with means–ends analysis and calls the result a sub-problem, which is the product of decomposition, not of abstraction.

questions.q: An examination has 50 questions. Four marks are awarded for each correct response and two marks are deducted for each wrong one. Bridget is said to have scored 165. Taking *c* as the number of correct responses, which conclusion is right?
options: The score must equal 6*c* − 100, which is always even, so 165 is impossible and the data are inconsistent
*c* = 44.17, so Bridget gave about 44 correct responses
*c* = 44, because 6*c* − 100 comes closest to 165 when *c* = 44
*c* = 41.25, because 165 divided by 4 gives the number of correct responses
questions.why: Why A is right: with *c* correct, wrong = 50 − *c*, so the score is 4*c* − 2(50 − *c*) = 6*c* − 100. That is always even, and 165 is odd, so no whole number of correct responses gives 165. The data are inconsistent. *(The achievable scores nearest 165 are 164 at c = 44 and 170 at c = 45. With a 1-mark penalty the answer would be exactly 43, almost certainly what was intended. Never write 44.17.)* Why the others are wrong: B is 265/6, the arithmetic the slide invites, and a number of correct answers cannot be fractional · C rounds a fractional answer to an integer and calls the mismatch acceptable · D ignores the two-mark penalty entirely and divides the score by 4.

questions.q: Before a problem can be solved with a computational approach, three factors must be considered. They are:
options: The problem must be routine; it must be well defined; and an algorithm must already exist
The problem must be clearly defined; it must be computable; and its data requirements must be examined
The problem must be decidable; it must be solvable; and it must be a decision problem
The inputs must be known; the process must be known; and the output must be known
questions.why: Why B is right: the three factors are that the problem be clearly defined, that it be computable, and that its data requirements be examined. Why the others are wrong: A imports "routine", which is a week 2 problem type, and demands an algorithm already exist, which is what the approach is meant to produce · C substitutes the computability vocabulary of week 2 for the three factors · D is the input–process–output triple from understanding a problem in week 1.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six basic computational methods?
options: Pipelining
Divide and conquer
Visualisation
Backtracking
questions.why: Why B is right: divide and conquer is one of the five **sophisticated** approaches, not one of the six basic computational methods. Why the others are wrong: A, C and D are all basic methods, alongside problem recognition, data mining and performance testing.

questions.q: In the Week 3 list of computational methods, _______ deals with evaluating whether a program works as expected or not before it is released, and using that knowledge to make it more effective.
options: Performance testing
Data mining
Pipelining
Backtracking
questions.why: Why A is right: performance testing evaluates whether a system or program works as expected before release and uses that to make it more effective. Why the others are wrong: B extracts patterns from large data sets, not from a program's behaviour · C divides a task into subtasks whose results feed forward · D examines more than one possible solution and reverses to earlier states. Note that Week 12 uses the same name for a non-functional software-testing method concerned with load and network delay; that sense is not what is being defined here.

questions.q: Which approach breaks a problem into sub-problems and saves the solutions of the sub-problems so that they need not be computed again?
options: Divide and conquer
Backtracking
Dynamic programming
The greedy algorithm
questions.why: Why C is right: saving the sub-problem solutions so they need not be recomputed is the defining feature of dynamic programming; "saved" is the marker word. Why the others are wrong: A splits and recombines but never stores results for reuse — that is the whole difference between the two · B examines options and backtracks, without storing anything for reuse · D makes the best choice at each stage and never reconsiders, so there is nothing to save.

questions.q: Hypothesis: a new teaching method improves student pass rates. What is the corresponding null hypothesis?
options: The new teaching method reduces student pass rates
The new teaching method improves student pass rates more than any other method
Student pass rates cannot be measured reliably
The new teaching method does not improve student pass rates
questions.why: Why D is right: the null hypothesis is the no-effect version. Take the hypothesis and negate the effect. Why the others are wrong: A states the *opposite* effect rather than no effect, the commonest mistake · B strengthens the original hypothesis instead of negating it · C is a statement about measurement, not a hypothesis about the effect at all.

questions.q: Which pair of conditions must hold for divide and conquer to be effective?
options: The smaller parts must all be of equal size, and each must be solved by recursion
Solving the original problem directly must be less complicated than combining the solutions of the smaller easier parts
The solutions of the smaller parts must be saved so that they are never recomputed
The smaller parts must be simpler than the original problem, and combining their solutions must be less complicated than solving the original directly
questions.why: Why D is right: the smaller parts must be simpler than the original, **and** combining their solutions must be less complicated than solving the original directly. If combining were harder, dividing would never pay. Why the others are wrong: A adds an equal-size requirement and a recursion requirement that the course does not state · B is the slide's own wording, which is backwards — if it were true you would never divide at all · C is the dynamic programming condition, not the divide-and-conquer one.

questions.q: The numbers 2, 8, 4, 9 and 3 are sorted into descending order using merge sort. What is the final list?
questions.why: Why A is right: dividing gives [2],[8] and [4],[9],[3]; merging by repeatedly taking the larger front element gives [9,3], then [9,4,3], then [8,2], and finally 9, 8, 4, 3, 2. Why the others are wrong: B sorts ascending, ignoring "descending order" · C is the two halves concatenated without merging at all · D merges the tail wrongly, leaving 2 before 3 in a descending list.

questions.q: Six activities have start times 2, 4, 1, 6, 9 and 6 and finish times 3, 5, 7, 8, 10 and 10 respectively. Only one activity can be worked on at a time. Applying the greedy rule of always taking the available activity that finishes earliest, how many activities can be performed?
questions.why: Why B is right: sorted by finish time the activities are A(2,3), B(4,5), C(1,7), D(6,8), E(9,10), F(6,10). Take A (time 3), take B (time 5), skip C because it starts at 1, take D (time 8), take E (time 10), skip F. That is four: A, B, D and E. Why the others are wrong: A drops one of the four, usually E, by mistakenly treating a start time of 9 as clashing with a finish time of 8 · C admits C or F, both of which overlap an activity already taken · D ignores the one-at-a-time constraint altogether.

questions.q: A padlock has four positions, each holding a digit from 0 to 9. A brute-force attack tries every combination in turn. What are the worst-case and average numbers of attempts?
options: 40 and 20
questions.why: Why C is right: four positions with ten digits each give 10⁴ = 10,000 combinations. The worst case is 10,000 attempts and the average is half of that, 5,000. Why the others are wrong: A multiplies 4 by 10 instead of raising 10 to the fourth power · B counts permutations of distinct digits (10 × 9 × 8 × 7), although digits may repeat · D is the five-digit lock, 10⁵.

questions.q: A test is carried out at a significance level of 0.05 and returns a p-value of 0.03. According to the decision rule taught in this course, what follows?
options: The null hypothesis is rejected, because the p-value is less than the significance level
The null hypothesis is accepted, because the p-value is small
The null hypothesis is rejected, and it is now proved that the effect exists
The null hypothesis is accepted, because a 5% risk of error still remains
questions.why: Why A is right: when the p-value is less than or equal to the significance level, the null hypothesis is rejected. Here 0.03 ≤ 0.05. *(In a written answer add that we strictly "fail to reject" rather than "accept" when the p-value is high.)* Why the others are wrong: B applies the rule backwards, accepting on a small p-value · C draws the right conclusion for the wrong reason: rejecting is never a proof, only evidence · D confuses the significance level with a reason to accept.

questions.q: Which sequence gives the algorithm development steps in the correct order?
options: Problem analysis; problem description; high-level algorithm development; algorithm refinement; algorithm review
Problem description; problem analysis; algorithm refinement; high-level algorithm development; algorithm review
Problem description; problem analysis; high-level algorithm development; algorithm refinement; algorithm review
Problem description; high-level algorithm development; problem analysis; algorithm review; algorithm refinement
questions.why: Why C is right: the five steps are problem description, problem analysis, high-level algorithm development, algorithm refinement, algorithm review. Why the others are wrong: A analyses before describing, so there is nothing to analyse · B refines before there is a high-level algorithm to refine · D pushes analysis behind development and puts review before refinement.

questions.q: Three issues can arise while obtaining a problem description. They are:
options: Syntax errors, logical errors and run-time errors
Best case, worst case and average case
Sequence, selection and repetition
Unstated assumptions, ambiguity and incompleteness
questions.why: Why D is right: the three issues in obtaining a problem description are unstated assumptions, ambiguity and incompleteness. Why the others are wrong: A is the three error types from week 1 · B is the three complexity cases · C is the three representation structures.

questions.q: The refined algorithm for finding a maximum loops until the user enters a sentinel value; on each pass it prompts for a number, allows the user to type it in, compares it with the current maximum, and adds 1 to a counter. The user enters 12, 47, 9, 63 and 30, then the sentinel −1. What are the final maximum and the final counter value?
options: Maximum 63, counter 6
Maximum 63, counter 5
Maximum 47, counter 5
Maximum 30, counter 6
questions.why: Why B is right: 12 becomes the maximum; 47 replaces it; 9 does not; 63 replaces it; 30 does not; then −1 is the sentinel and the loop ends. Maximum 63, and the counter, incremented once per number actually processed, is 5. Why the others are wrong: A counts the sentinel as a sixth number, but the sentinel signals the end and is not processed · C stops at 47, missing the later replacement by 63 · D reports the last value entered instead of the largest, and counts the sentinel.

questions.q: How do priori and posterior analysis differ?
options: Priori analysis is carried out after implementation and deals with space and running time; posterior analysis is carried out before implementation
Priori analysis is carried out before implementation and does not directly affect it; posterior analysis is carried out after implementation and deals with actual space and running time requirements
Priori analysis deals with space requirements while posterior analysis deals with time requirements
Both are carried out after implementation, priori on the algorithm and posterior on the finished program
questions.why: Why B is right: priori analysis is carried out before implementation and does not directly affect it; posterior analysis is carried out after and deals with actual space and running time. Why the others are wrong: A swaps before and after · C swaps *space* and *time* onto the two analyses; both belong to posterior analysis · D places both after implementation, which erases the distinction.

questions.q: What is best case time complexity?
options: The time the algorithm requires for the smallest input it can accept
The time the algorithm requires for a typical input of size n
The minimum time that the algorithm will require for an input of size n
The time required by the fastest available algorithm for that problem
questions.why: Why C is right: best case time complexity is the minimum time the algorithm will require for an input of size n. Why the others are wrong: A reads "best case" as "smallest input", the classic misreading; the input size is fixed at n · B is the average case definition · D compares algorithms rather than inputs, which is not what the three cases measure.

questions.q: Which sequence lists the growth rates in the order given in the course, from slowest-growing to fastest-growing?
options: C, Log N, (Log N)², N, N Log N, N², N³, 2ⁿ
C, Log N, N, (Log N)², N Log N, N², 2ⁿ, N³
C, N, Log N, (Log N)², N Log N, N², N³, 2ⁿ
C, Log N, (Log N)², N, N², N Log N, N³, 2ⁿ
questions.why: Why A is right: the order taught is C, Log N, (Log N)², N, N Log N, N², N³, 2ⁿ. *(The PDF lost superscripts: "Log2 N" is (Log N)² and "2N" is 2ⁿ.)* Why the others are wrong: B puts N before (Log N)² and lets 2ⁿ overtake N³ too early · C puts N ahead of Log N, reversing the two slowest-growing non-constant terms · D puts N² before N Log N, the pairing students most often invert.

questions.q:
What is the time complexity of the loop below?
```
i = n
WHILE i > 1
    i = i / 2
ENDWHILE
```
options: O(n)
O(log log n)
O(log n)
questions.why: Why D is right: the loop variable is divided by a constant amount on each pass, which the course gives as O(log n). Why the others are wrong: A would need no loop at all · B applies when the loop variable is incremented or decremented by a constant amount, not divided · C applies when the loop variable is reduced or increased *exponentially*, a step beyond halving.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the characteristics of a good algorithm?
options: Finiteness
Unambiguity
Modularity
Language independence
questions.why: Why C is right: modularity is one of the **design considerations**, not one of the characteristics. The characteristics are input, unambiguity, finiteness, effectiveness and language independence. *(The slides list only four, omitting effectiveness; the summary lists five. This key uses the summary's five.)* Why the others are wrong: A, B and D are all characteristics — limited and countable instructions, clear instructions, and independence of any programming language.

questions.q: In algorithm representation, which structure covers steps that are executed only when a condition is satisfied?
options: Sequence
Selection
Repetition
Recursion
questions.why: Why B is right: selection covers steps executed only when a condition is satisfied, with one or more alternatives. Why the others are wrong: A is the ordered step-by-step structure with nothing skipped · C is the repeated execution of the same steps · D is not one of the three representation structures at all; it belongs to week 10.

questions.q: A flowchart reads two numbers, adds them, prints the result and stops. In order, which symbols does it use?
options: Oval, rectangle, parallelogram, rectangle, oval
Oval, parallelogram, diamond, parallelogram, oval
Parallelogram, rectangle, diamond, parallelogram, oval
Oval, parallelogram, rectangle, parallelogram, oval
questions.why: Why D is right: START is an oval, reading two numbers is a parallelogram (input/output), adding them is a rectangle (process), printing the result is a parallelogram, and STOP is an oval. Why the others are wrong: A uses a rectangle for input and output, the commonest shape error · B uses a diamond for the addition, although no yes/no question is asked · C omits the start oval, breaking the principle that a flowchart must have a start point.

questions.q: The _______ symbol is used in complex flowcharts to connect independent elements across multiple pages.
options: Link connector
On-page connector
Declaration
Flow line
questions.why: Why A is right: the link (off-page) connector, drawn as a pentagon, connects independent elements across multiple pages. Why the others are wrong: B works across a **single** page only — the exact pairing this question tests · C, the declaration or predefined process symbol, shows a complex or well-known operation · D simply shows the direction of flow.

questions.q: Which pairing of flowchart symbol and purpose is correct?
options: A cylinder shows the combining of various paths into a single path
A pentagon connects independent elements across a single page
A rectangle with a wavy bottom edge shows a complex or well-known operation
An elongated hexagon shows the difference between steps that prepare for work and steps that actually work
questions.why: Why D is right: the elongated hexagon is the preparation symbol, distinguishing steps that prepare for work from steps that do the work. Why the others are wrong: A gives the cylinder the merge symbol's job; the cylinder is the database, and merging is a downward triangle · B gives the pentagon the on-page connector's job; the pentagon crosses pages · C gives the wavy-bottom rectangle the predefined-process job; the wavy-bottom rectangle is a document, and predefined process is a rectangle with double side bars.

questions.q: A _______ flowchart ensures that the communication gap between the users and the developers of a system is reduced.
options: Process
Data
Workflow
Swimlane
questions.why: Why B is right: the data flowchart shows the flow of information and reduces the communication gap between users and developers. Why the others are wrong: A describes how a process is completed in an organisation · C describes the manner in which businesses function · D shows multiple information flows side by side.

questions.q: What distinguishes a swimlane flowchart from a workflow flowchart?
options: It allows the creation of multiple categories of activities shown side by side
It shows the flow of information in the data-processing aspect of system design
It describes the manner in which businesses function
It can be applied to almost anything and quickly describes how a process is completed
questions.why: Why A is right: the swimlane's distinguishing feature is that it allows multiple categories of activities to be shown side by side. Why the others are wrong: B describes the data flowchart · C describes the workflow flowchart, the one swimlane is most often confused with · D describes the process flowchart.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of flowcharts?
options: They ensure that the logic of a process or program is simplified
They are added to program specification documents so that other programmers can follow the logic
Their logic can make a program unnecessarily longer than normal
They are used to ascertain whether the logic of a program works
questions.why: Why C is right: flowchart logic is hardly the most efficient basis for writing a program because it can make the program unnecessarily longer than normal. Why the others are wrong: A, B and D are the three listed **advantages** — simplified logic, inclusion in specification documents, and confirming that the logic works.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the principles for drawing a flowchart?
options: Every flowchart should fit on a single page
The flowchart should have a start point and a stop point
Flow lines should generally not cross if possible
Instructions for comparisons should be made as simple as possible
questions.why: Why A is right: nothing in the principles requires a single page. Indeed a listed *disadvantage* is that complex processes may need a flowchart spanning multiple pages, which is why the off-page connector exists. Why the others are wrong: B, C and D are three of the four principles; the fourth is that the flowchart be easy to follow, neat and clear.

questions.q: In the sum-of-numbers flowchart, Sum and Count are both set to 0; on each pass a number *n* is entered, Sum becomes Sum + *n*, Count becomes Count + 1, and the decision returns the flow to the input step while its condition is true. The decision is changed from `Is Count < 5` to `Is Count <= 5`, and the numbers 4, 7, 2, 9, 6 and 8 are entered in that order. What is printed?
questions.why: Why D is right: with `Is Count <= 5` the loop returns to the input step while Count is 5 or less, so it exits only after Count reaches 6. Six numbers are read: 4 + 7 + 2 + 9 + 6 + 8 = 36. Why the others are wrong: A stops after four numbers (4 + 7 + 2 + 9), an off-by-one in the other direction · B skips the first input, treating `Sum = 0` as consuming a number (7 + 2 + 9 + 6) · C is the total for the *original* `Count < 5` test, five numbers — the answer given by anyone who does not notice the change.

questions.q: Which statement about pseudocode is correct?
options: It is the graphical representation of the sequence of operations in a computer program
It must follow the syntax of a specific programming language so that it can be compiled
It is the textual representation of an algorithm and cannot be compiled or executed
It is derived from a flowchart, so the flowchart must always be drawn first
questions.why: Why C is right: pseudocode is the textual representation of an algorithm; it looks like a program but cannot be compiled or executed. Why the others are wrong: A gives pseudocode the flowchart's definition — the week 6 mid-lesson question turns on exactly this, and the answer there is "No" · B contradicts the rule that pseudocode be language independent · D reproduces the summary's claim that pseudocode is "a transition from flowcharts"; the two are independent representations of the same algorithm, and neither derives from the other.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the pseudocode rules given in the lecture slides?
options: Each line should contain only one statement
Every construct must be indented to show where its body begins and ends
Keywords should be written in capital letters
Statements should be language independent
questions.why: Why B is right: the slides give three rules only — one statement per line, keywords in capitals, and language independence. Indentation is a convention from the wider literature, not a rule stated in this course. *(The week 6 summary says there are four rules but never names a fourth. If a question demands a number, the examiner may key four.)* Why the others are wrong: A, C and D are the three stated rules.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the eight pseudocode constructs?
options: EXCEPTION and WHEN
GOTO
REPEAT-UNTIL
CALL
questions.why: Why B is right: `goto` is a C statement from week 9, the example of unconditional branching. It is not one of the eight pseudocode constructs. Why the others are wrong: A, C and D are all constructs, along with SEQUENCE, CASE, WHILE, FOR and IF-THEN-ELSE.

questions.q: Which line correctly closes a REPEAT construct?
options: UNTIL condition
ENDFOR condition
ENDREPEAT
ENDWHILE condition
questions.why: Why A is right: REPEAT is closed by `UNTIL condition`, with the condition set at the ending or bottom of the construct. Why the others are wrong: B is the slide's own typo, borrowing FOR's closing keyword for a REPEAT loop — the single most copied error in week 6 · C invents a keyword by analogy with ENDFOR and ENDWHILE · D closes it with WHILE's keyword, which belongs to a loop testing its condition at the top.

questions.q: In the seven steps to writing a pseudocode, which step comes immediately after the identification of main steps?
options: Problem definition
Using constructs to describe logic
Using variables and data structures
Header writing
questions.why: Why D is right: the seven steps run problem definition, identification of main steps, **header writing**, using variables and data structures, using constructs to describe logic, using clear and concise language, testing and refining. Why the others are wrong: A comes *before* identification of main steps, not after · B is step 5, two steps too late · C is step 4, one step too late — the step most often mistaken for third, because writing a header feels like documentation rather than development.

questions.q: What must a pseudocode header include?
options: The inputs, the process and the expected outputs of a test
The variables to be used and their data types
The name of the algorithm, a short description of its purpose, and a list of the required inputs and outputs
The name of the algorithm, the name of its author and the date it was written
questions.why: Why C is right: the header must contain the algorithm's name, a short description of its purpose, and a list of the required inputs and outputs. Why the others are wrong: A is what a **test case** specifies, from week 12 · B is step 4 of writing a pseudocode, not the header · D is ordinary file metadata; the course requires the purpose and the input/output list, not the author and the date.

questions.q: _______ can be written in any notation or language, while _______ are written in a combination of natural and programming language elements.
options: Pseudocode … Algorithms
Flowcharts … Algorithms
Algorithms … Pseudocode
Algorithms … Flowcharts
questions.why: Why C is right: algorithms can be written in any notation or language; pseudocode is written in a combination of natural and programming language elements. Why the others are wrong: A reverses the pair, the error the week 6 mid-lesson question is designed to catch · B substitutes flowcharts for algorithms in the first blank · D substitutes flowcharts for pseudocode in the second, although flowcharts are graphical, not textual.

questions.q:
What is printed by the pseudocode below?
```
SET total = 0
SET k = 1
WHILE k <= 4
    COMPUTE total = total + (k * k)
    INCREMENT k
ENDWHILE
PRINT total
```
questions.why: Why D is right: k = 1 gives total 1; k = 2 gives 5; k = 3 gives 14; k = 4 gives 30; k becomes 5 and the condition `k <= 4` fails. 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30. Why the others are wrong: A reports only the last term added, 4 × 4 · B computes k × 2 instead of k × k (2 + 4 + 6 + 8) · C runs the loop one pass too far, to k = 5, adding 25.

questions.q: The examination pseudocode initialises passes and failures to zero, reads each result in turn, adds one to passes for a pass and one to failures for a fail, prints both counts, and then prints "increase tuition" if seven or more students passed. The ten results, in order, are P F F P P F P P F P. What is the output?
options: passes 6, failures 4, and "increase tuition" is printed
passes 6, failures 4, and "increase tuition" is not printed
passes 4, failures 6, and "increase tuition" is not printed
passes 7, failures 3, and "increase tuition" is printed
questions.why: Why B is right: the sequence P F F P P F P P F P holds six passes (positions 1, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10) and four failures (positions 2, 3, 6, 9). Six is fewer than seven, so "increase tuition" is not printed. *(The lecture's problem statement says "more than seven" while its pseudocode tests "seven or more"; at six passes both readings agree.)* Why the others are wrong: A gets the counts right but applies the tuition test backwards · C swaps the pass and fail counts · D miscounts the passes as seven, and then prints on a condition six does not meet.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of pseudocode?
options: There are no generally accepted standards, so everyone can write it in their own way
Special software is needed in order to write and store it
Once it has been written it cannot easily be modified
It is more visual than a flowchart, which makes the logic harder to follow
questions.why: Why A is right: pseudocode has no generally accepted standards, so everyone writes it their own way, leading to varied styles and possible complications. Why the others are wrong: B reverses the listed advantage that no special software is needed — any text editor will do · C reverses the listed advantage that pseudocode can easily be modified · D reverses the actual disadvantage: pseudocode is *less* visual than a flowchart, which is why it takes longer to read.

questions.q: Besides instructions, what does a computer program contain?
options: Data and the various memory addresses in which the instructions work
Header files and the libraries that they import
Comments and the program documentation
Nothing else; a program is only a series of instructions
questions.why: Why A is right: a program includes more than instructions — it also contains data and the various memory addresses in which the instructions work. Why the others are wrong: B names files used to build the program, not what the program itself contains · C names documentation, which is a separate deliverable and, in the case of comments, is stripped before execution · D denies the "more than just instructions" sentence the course states outright.

questions.q: What are the three basic data types in the C language?
options: Integers, floating-point numbers and Booleans
Characters, integers and floating-point numbers
Characters, strings and integers
Integers, arrays and structures
questions.why: Why B is right: the three basic types in C are characters, integers and floating-point numbers. Why the others are wrong: A imports Booleans; `bool` exists in C, but the three *basic* types do not include it, and Boolean values are returned as integers anyway · C imports strings, which C represents with character arrays rather than a basic type · D lists two composite structures, arrays and structures, alongside one basic type.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the six types of operator provided by C?
options: Bitwise
Assignment
Misc
Iterative
questions.why: Why D is right: there is no "iterative" operator category. The six are arithmetic, relational, logical, bitwise, assignment and misc. Why the others are wrong: A, B and C are three of the six. Bitwise and misc are the two most often forgotten, which is why they appear here as tempting answers.

questions.q: To which categories do the operators `&& || !` and `& | ^` belong, in that order?
options: Bitwise and logical
Relational and logical
Logical and bitwise
Logical and assignment
questions.why: Why C is right: `&& || !` are the logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) and `& | ^` are the bitwise operators (bitwise AND, OR, XOR). Why the others are wrong: A reverses the two, the single commonest operator confusion in C · B calls `&&` relational; the relational operators are `== != > < >= <=` · D calls `&` an assignment operator; the assignment set is `= += -= *= /= %=`.

questions.q: Which statement about variable names and computer memory is correct?
options: Variable names are stored in memory next to the values that they hold
Variable names are stored in a CPU register for as long as the program runs
Variable names are stored in memory, and the compiler discards the memory addresses
Variable names are not stored inside the computer memory; the compiler replaces them with memory location addresses
questions.why: Why D is right: variable names are not stored inside the computer memory; the compiler replaces them with memory location addresses. This is the week 7 sentence to reproduce verbatim. Why the others are wrong: A keeps the names in memory, which is exactly what the course denies · B relocates them to a register, still storing them · C keeps the names and discards the addresses, an exact inversion of what happens.

questions.q: How are a variable definition and a variable declaration related?
options: Every declaration is a definition, but not every definition is a declaration
A declaration sets aside the storage, while a definition only states that a name exists
Every definition is also a declaration, but not every declaration is a definition
A definition and a declaration are two names for exactly the same statement
questions.why: Why C is right: a variable definition is also a declaration, but not all declarations are definitions — a declaration says a name exists with a given type; a definition also sets aside the storage. Why the others are wrong: A inverts the containment · B swaps the two roles, giving storage allocation to the declaration · D erases the distinction the course draws explicitly.

questions.q: In programming, the state of an object is stored in _______ and the behaviour of an object is described by _______.
options: variables … methods
methods … variables
classes … structures
unions … functions
questions.why: Why A is right: the state of an object is stored in variables and the behaviour of an object is described by methods. Why the others are wrong: B swaps them, the error the course warns about directly · C names two ways of grouping data, neither of which is where state or behaviour lives · D names a C construct and a code unit rather than the object's two components.

questions.q: What distinguishes a union from a structure in C?
options: A union can group items of only one type, while a structure can group items of different types
All the members of a union start at the same location in memory, and a union variable can represent the value of only one of its members at a time
Each member of a union has its own memory location, while the members of a structure all share one
The members of a union are reached with the dot syntax, while those of a structure are not
questions.why: Why B is right: all the members of a union start at the same location in memory, and a union variable can represent the value of only one of its members at a time. Why the others are wrong: A invents a same-type restriction; a union, like a structure, groups items of possibly different types · C swaps the memory behaviour of the two — separate locations belong to the structure · D is false of both: members of a structure and of a union are alike reached with the dot syntax.

questions.q: Data encapsulation is best described as:
options: grouping items of possibly different types into a single user-defined type
storing all the members of an object at the same memory address
hiding the implementation details of an object from the user, who interacts with it only through a set of public methods
replacing variable names with memory location addresses when the program is compiled
questions.why: Why C is right: data encapsulation is hiding the implementation details of an object from the user, so the user interacts only through public methods while the internals stay hidden. Access is controlled by the specifiers `public` and `private`. *(The slides show this with a `class Dog`, written as though `class` were a C construct. C has no classes; they belong to C++.)* Why the others are wrong: A is the definition of a **structure** · B is the memory behaviour of a **union** · D is the week 7 sentence about variable names and memory addresses, which concerns the compiler, not encapsulation.

questions.q: What is abstraction?
options: The process of hiding the internal details of an application from the outer world
The process of dividing a program's functionality into independent modules
The process of modifying a system to improve its internal structure without changing its external behaviour
The process of grouping items of possibly different types into a single type
questions.why: Why A is right: abstraction is the process of hiding the internal details of an application from the outer world. Why the others are wrong: B defines modularisation from week 11 · C defines refactoring · D defines a structure. All three are near neighbours of abstraction, which is why they are offered.

questions.q: A team publishes only a method's name, the format of its input and the format of its output; the code inside is never shown. Which has been implemented?
options: Data abstraction
Functional abstraction
Modularisation
Pipelining
questions.why: Why B is right: functional abstraction hides the implementation of an object's methods; other programs need to know only the method's name, the format of the input and the format of the output — the exact three items published here. Why the others are wrong: A hides the **data** of an object, not the implementation of its methods · C divides a program into independent modules, which is about structure, not about what is exposed · D chains subtask results together and has nothing to do with hiding anything.

questions.q: What are the two ways of implementing abstraction given in the lecture?
options: Comments and program documentation
Compilers and interpreters
Arrays and unions
Access specifiers and header files
questions.why: Why D is right: abstraction is implemented with access specifiers (`public` and `private`) and with header files, which let us use functions without knowing how they are implemented. Why the others are wrong: A names documentation, which describes a program rather than restricting access to it · B names translators, which convert code between languages · C names two data groupings, neither of which controls access.

questions.q: Which escape sequence represents a horizontal tab?
questions.why: Why B is right: `\t` is the horizontal tab. Why the others are wrong: A is the **vertical** tab, the neighbouring entry in the table and the one most often confused with it · C is backspace · D is carriage return, which is often mistaken for a whitespace-advancing sequence but returns to the start of the line.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the parts of a function definition?
options: The return type
The parameters
The function body
The header file in which the function is declared
questions.why: Why D is right: a function definition consists of a return type, a function name, parameters and a function body. Where the function is declared is not one of its parts. Why the others are wrong: A, B and C are three of the four parts; the fourth is the function name.

Why C is right: `max(3, 9)` tests `3 > 9`, which is false, so it returns 9; `max(7, 2)` tests `7 > 2`, which is true, so it returns 7. 9 + 7 = 16. Why the others are wrong: A takes the first argument each time (3 + 7), ignoring the comparison · B takes the second argument each time (9 + 2), the same error mirrored · D adds all four arguments, treating `max` as a sum. (The listing is shown inside main; written at file scope, as the deck prints it, int result = max(3, 9) + max(7, 2); will not compile — C requires a constant initialiser for an object with static storage duration.)

questions.q: How do modules differ from functions?
options: They differ in scale: a module is larger and can contain various functions and classes
A function returns a value while a module cannot return anything
A module is simply a function that has been written without any parameters
Functions are written by programmers while modules are generated by the compiler
questions.why: Why A is right: modules and functions are very similar; the main difference is scale — a module is used on a much larger scale and can contain various functions and classes. Why the others are wrong: B invents a return-value rule the course does not state · C confuses a module with a function that has no parameters; a function may indeed contain no parameters, but that does not make it a module · D invents an authorship distinction; both are written by programmers.

questions.q: Which statement about a compound statement (a block) is correct?
options: It contains more than one statement inside curly brackets, and the right curly bracket has no semicolon after it
It contains more than one statement inside curly brackets, and the right curly bracket must be followed by a semicolon
Simple statements are made from compound statements, which is why blocks are needed
It is used only when writing functions, never in decision-making or iterative statements
questions.why: Why A is right: a block contains more than one statement inside curly brackets, and the right curly bracket does not have a semicolon after it. Why the others are wrong: B adds the semicolon the course explicitly says is absent · C is the week 9 summary's own reversed sentence — a compound statement is made from simple statements, not the other way round · D leaves out two of the three places blocks are used; blocks appear in functions, decision-making statements and iterative statements.

options: NOT EQUAL, because 4 is not equal to 5
Nothing, because the condition is not a comparison and so nothing is evaluated
EQUAL, because the assignment gives `a` the value 5, and any nonzero value counts as true
EQUAL, because `a` and `b` both still hold 4
questions.why: Why C is right: `a = b + 1` is an assignment, not a comparison. It stores 5 in `a` and the expression evaluates to 5. Since any number that is not 0 counts as true, the `if` branch runs and EQUAL is printed. Why the others are wrong: A reads `=` as `==`, the commonest C error, and then evaluates the comparison it wishes had been written · B assumes a non-comparison condition cannot be evaluated, although any expression may serve as a condition · D gets the printed word right for the wrong reason: `a` no longer holds 4 once the assignment has run.

questions.q: In C, which values are treated as true?
options: Only the literal `true`
Any number that is not 0
Only the value 1
Any positive number, but not negative numbers
questions.why: Why B is right: Boolean values are returned as integers, with 1 or any other number that is not 0 representing true and 0 representing false. Why the others are wrong: A restricts truth to the literal, ignoring the integer rule · C restricts it to 1 alone, dropping every other nonzero value · D excludes negative numbers, although any nonzero value — negative included — is true.

questions.q: Which statement about branching is correct?
options: `goto` is an example of conditional branching, because control moves only when a label is reached
`if-else` is an example of unconditional branching, because one of the two blocks always runs
`switch` is an example of unconditional branching, because it executes one code block among many
`goto` is an example of unconditional branching, because it moves program control without checking any condition
questions.why: Why D is right: `goto` is the lecture's example of unconditional branching precisely because it specifies no condition before moving program control. Why the others are wrong: A calls `goto` conditional; reaching a label is not a condition being tested · B calls `if-else` unconditional, although where control moves depends entirely on whether the condition is satisfied · C calls `switch` unconditional, although it selects a block by testing an expression.

questions.q: The lecture's summary slide states that there are exactly three types of decision-making statement. Which of the following is NOT one of the three it names?
options: `if`
`if-else`
`if-else-if`
`switch`
questions.why: Why D is right: the lecture names exactly three decision-making statements — `if`, `if-else` and `if-else-if` — and introduces `switch` separately as a statement that executes one code block among many alternatives. *(Some marking schemes count `switch` as a fourth decision-making statement, so note the wording of the question you are given.)* Why the others are wrong: A, B and C are the three types the lecture names.

options: Both print nothing
The `while` loop prints nothing; the `do-while` loop prints 9
Both print 9
The `while` loop prints 9; the `do-while` loop prints nothing
questions.why: Why B is right: the `while` loop tests `9 <= 5` before its first pass, which is false, so nothing is printed. The `do-while` loop executes its body first and tests afterwards, so it prints 9 before finding `10 <= 5` false. Why the others are wrong: A forgets that a `do-while` loop is guaranteed to execute at least once · C treats both loops as bottom-tested · D swaps the two loops, giving the top-tested behaviour to `do-while`.

Why C is right: `i` runs 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and `total` accumulates 2, 6, 12, 20, 30. The printed value is 30. Why the others are wrong: A sums `i` itself and forgets the multiplication by 2 · B stops at `i = 4`, reading `i <= 5` as `i < 5` · D runs a sixth pass at `i = 6`, adding 12 — the mirror-image off-by-one.

questions.q: Which statement about an array is correct?
options: It stores a fixed-size sequential collection of elements of the same type
It groups items of possibly different types into a single user-defined type
All of its elements start at the same location in memory
Its size grows automatically as more elements are added to it
questions.why: Why A is right: an array stores a fixed-size sequential collection of elements of the same type. The three marked words are fixed-size, sequential and same type. Why the others are wrong: B is the definition of a **structure**, whose members may be of different types · C is the memory behaviour of a **union** · D contradicts "fixed-size"; an array's size is set at declaration.

Why C is right: indexing starts at 0, so `salaries[0]` is 1000.0, `salaries[1]` is 2.0 and `salaries[2]` is 3.4. Why the others are wrong: A takes index 2 as the second item counted from 1 in the wrong direction, landing on the first · B counts from 1 rather than 0, the standard off-by-one · D counts from 1 in the other direction, landing one past the answer.

options: Nothing, because the element must be written as `grid[1,2]`
questions.why: Why B is right: `grid[1]` is the second row, `{4, 5, 6}`, and `[2]` selects its third element, 6. Why the others are wrong: A reads `grid[1][2]` as row 0, taking the first row's third element · C counts within the row from 1 rather than 0 · D claims the comma form is required, when in fact each subscript must be enclosed in its own pair of square brackets and `grid[1,2]` is what is wrong.

Why A is right: `i` runs 1, 2, 3, 4 — it stops before 5 — so the sum is `arr[1] + arr[2] + arr[3] + arr[4]` = 9 + 2 + 7 + 5 = 23. Why the others are wrong: B runs `i` to 5 inclusive, adding `arr[5]` = 3 · C starts at `i = 0`, adding `arr[0]` = 4 · D does both, summing the whole array.

questions.q: Every recursive function has two components. They are:
options: A function header and a function body
A declaration and a definition
A direct call and an indirect call
A base case and a recursive case
questions.why: Why D is right: every recursive function has a base case, which handles the situation where there is nothing left to do, and a recursive case, which breaks the problem into a smaller version of itself. Why the others are wrong: A names the two parts of a **function definition**, which every function has, recursive or not · B names the two ways a function is introduced to the compiler · C names two of the four **types** of recursion, not its two components.

Why A is right: `f(7)` = 7 × `f(5)`; `f(5)` = 5 × `f(3)`; `f(3)` = 3 × `f(1)`; `f(1)` hits the base case and returns 1. Unwinding gives 3, then 15, then 105. Why the others are wrong: B stops one level early at 7 × 5 · C continues past the base case to include a factor of 2, as though the base were `n <= 0` · D computes 7!, subtracting 1 rather than 2 at each call.

questions.q: A recursive function ends with the line `return n * fact(n - 1);`. How is this recursion classified, and why?
options: Tail recursion, because the recursive call is the last thing written on the line
Direct recursion, because a multiplication is still pending when the call returns
Indirect recursion, because the multiplication is carried out outside the function
Non-tail recursion, because a multiplication is still pending when the recursive call returns
questions.why: Why D is right: tail and non-tail turn on whether operations remain pending on return. The multiplication by `n` cannot be carried out until the recursive call returns, so it is non-tail. Why the others are wrong: A judges by where the call is written rather than by what is still waiting to happen · B gives the right *reason* but the wrong classification: direct and indirect describe **who makes the call**, not what is pending · C misapplies "indirect", which requires a second function that eventually calls back.

questions.q: In the general approach to writing recursive programs, which of the five steps comes last?
options: Writing the recursive calls that solve the subproblems
Writing the base case or cases
Decomposing the problem into subproblems
Writing code to combine, augment or modify the results of the recursive calls
questions.why: Why B is right: the five steps run header, decompose into subproblems, write recursive calls, combine or modify results, and finally write base case(s) for situations the recursive portion does not handle properly. Why the others are wrong: A is step 3 · C is step 2 · D is step 4. The trap in this question is the intuition that a base case must be written first because it executes last; in the course's method it is written last, once you know what the recursive portion leaves unhandled.

questions.q: What is modularisation?
options: Hiding the internal details of an application from the outer world
Modifying a software system to improve the internal structure of its design without changing its external behaviour
Dividing a program's functionality into independent modules, such that each module has everything it needs to implement only a part of that functionality
Grouping items of possibly different types into a single user-defined type
questions.why: Why C is right: modularisation is dividing a program's functionality into independent modules, such that each independent module has everything it needs to implement only a part of the program's functionality. Why the others are wrong: A defines abstraction · B defines refactoring · D defines a structure.

questions.q: What does good module independence require?
options: Low cohesion within a module and high coupling between modules
High cohesion within a module and low coupling between modules
High cohesion within a module and high coupling between modules
Low cohesion within a module and low coupling between modules
questions.why: Why B is right: cohesion measures how far the functions inside a module work together, and we want it high; coupling measures how far modules depend on one another, and we want it low. Why the others are wrong: A inverts both, the standard swap · C wants high coupling, which destroys module independence · D wants low cohesion, which means a module doing several unrelated jobs.

questions.q: Which of the following is a disadvantage of modularisation?
options: Smaller modules and functions are easier to understand
Modules and functions can be reused in another program
Compilation and loading time may be longer
Large programs can be written by several different people
questions.why: Why C is right: longer compilation and loading time is one of the five listed disadvantages, alongside longer execution time, increased storage, more inter-module communication problems and more initial design time. Why the others are wrong: A, B and D are all listed **advantages**. Every disadvantage of modularisation is a cost; every advantage is a gain in manageability or reuse.

questions.q: Which statement about structural partitioning is correct?
options: In horizontal partitioning, control modules at the top do the decision-making while worker modules below do all input, computation and output
In vertical partitioning, more data must be passed across the module interface, which makes the control flow more complex
In horizontal partitioning, the functionality is distributed among the modules in a top-down manner
In vertical partitioning, control modules at the top do the decision-making and little processing, while worker modules at the low level perform all input, computation and output
questions.why: Why D is right: vertical partitioning distributes functionality top-down, with control modules at the top making decisions and doing little processing while worker modules at the low level perform all input, computation and output. Why the others are wrong: A gives the control/worker split to horizontal partitioning · B gives horizontal partitioning's cost — more data across the module interface — to vertical · C describes top-down distribution but attaches it to horizontal partitioning.

questions.q: Which description of a software pattern is correct?
options: An idiom is a low-level, programming-language-specific pattern, often termed a coding pattern
An architectural pattern is a medium-level pattern, often considered equivalent to software components
A design pattern is a high-level pattern, often considered equivalent to software architecture
An idiom is a high-level pattern that defines subsystems, components and classes
questions.why: Why A is right: idioms are low-level, programming-language-specific patterns, often termed coding patterns. Why the others are wrong: B demotes the architectural pattern to medium level and gives it the design pattern's equivalence to software components · C promotes the design pattern to high level and gives it the architectural pattern's equivalence to software architecture · D promotes the idiom to high level and hands it the architectural pattern's job of defining subsystems, components and classes.

questions.q: When is bottom-up design described as more suitable?
options: When the software solution must be designed from scratch and the specific details are unknown
When the whole system is taken as one entity and decomposed repeatedly until the lowest level is reached
When the design starts with a generalised model and keeps defining the more specific parts of it
When a system is created from an existing system whose basic primitives can be reused
questions.why: Why D is right: bottom-up design starts with the most specific and basic components, so it suits a system created from an existing one whose basic primitives can be reused. Why the others are wrong: A is the condition under which **top-down** is more suitable · B describes top-down decomposition · C describes top-down design, which starts from a generalised model.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of information hiding?
options: It reduces the program's execution time
It emphasises communication through controlled interfaces
It decreases the probability of adverse effects
It restricts the effects of changes in one component on others
questions.why: Why A is right: information hiding costs execution time rather than saving it — longer execution time is a listed **disadvantage of modularisation**, not a benefit of hiding. Why the others are wrong: B, C and D are the three listed benefits: controlled interfaces, a decreased probability of adverse effects, and restricted effects of change.

questions.q: In the software testing life cycle, which phase comes immediately after test case development?
options: Test planning
Test execution
Test environment setup
Test cycle closure
questions.why: Why C is right: the six phases in order are requirement analysis, test planning, test case development, **test environment setup**, test execution and test cycle closure. Why the others are wrong: A is phase 2, one before test case development, not after · B is phase 5, skipping the environment setup — the phase people forget most often · D is phase 6, the last of all.

questions.q: What does a test case specify?
options: The testing strategy, the cost and the duration
The test inputs, the process and the expected outputs
The software and hardware requirements for the test
The entry point and the exit point of each testing phase
questions.why: Why B is right: a test case gives detailed step-by-step instructions on how a test should be performed, specifying the test inputs, the process and the expected outputs. Why the others are wrong: A is what the **test planning** phase defines · C is what the **test environment setup** phase specifies · D describes the entry and exit points that every phase has, not what a test case contains.

questions.q: A tester who has never seen the source code enters a 200-character password into a login form to check that the page does not crash. How is this test classified?
options: Functional, and white box
Non-functional, and white box
Non-functional, and black box
Functional, and black box
questions.why: Why C is right: a 200-character password checks robustness and resistance to crashing rather than whether a stated function computes correctly, so it is non-functional. Because the tester has never seen the source code, the internal structure is not known and the test is black box. Why the others are wrong: A and B both call the test white box, which requires the internal structure to be known to the tester · D calls it functional, which would fit "does a valid email and password admit the user?" but not a crash check.

questions.q: Which statement about testing methods is correct?
options: In white box testing the internal structure is known to the tester, who chooses inputs to exercise paths through the code
In black box testing the internal structure is known to the tester, who nevertheless tests only through the user interface
In grey box testing the internal structure is fully known, and the tests are conducted at the code level
In white box testing the internal structure is not known, which is why programming know-how is not needed
questions.why: Why A is right: in white box testing the internal structure, design and implementation are known to the tester, who chooses inputs to exercise paths through the code and determines the appropriate outputs. Why the others are wrong: B gives black box the white box definition; in black box testing the internal structure is **not** known · C makes grey box fully transparent, when it is partially known — internals for designing test cases, testing at the user level · D gives white box the black box definition and then denies the programming know-how the course calls essential.

questions.q: Grey box testing is primarily used in which type of testing?
options: Unit testing
Acceptance testing
System testing
Integration testing
questions.why: Why D is right: grey box testing is primarily used in integration testing. Why the others are wrong: A is where **white box** applies, along with integration and system testing · B is where **black box** applies, along with integration and system testing · C is applicable to both black and white box, but grey box is named as *primarily* integration.

questions.q: Which option names three widely used debuggers?
options: Debuggers, trace tools and profilers
Radare2, WinDbg and Valgrind
GCC, Clang and MSVC
Unit testing, integration testing and system testing
